title: Element distinctness: all pairs vs sorting
problem_statement: Given n integers a_1..a_n, decide whether they are pairwise distinct, i.e. whether a_i != a_j for all i < j. For n <= 1 the answer is yes.

input.size_measure: n integers; each comparison of two values costs O(1) (values have magnitude at most 10^18 in the harness).

algorithms.name: all pairs
algorithms.idea: Compare every pair of positions and answer no at the first equal pair.
algorithms.pseudocode: for i < j: if a_i == a_j: return no; return yes
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) worst case: exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons whenever the answer is yes

algorithms.name: sort, then compare neighbours
algorithms.idea: Sort a copy (bottom-up merge sort); equal values become adjacent, so the values are distinct iff no two neighbours are equal.
algorithms.pseudocode: b = merge_sort(a); return all(b[k-1] != b[k] for k in 1..n-1)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input (merge sort: ceil(log2 n) passes of Theta(n) each; final scan Theta(n))
algorithms.correctness: If a_i = a_j then, after sorting, every element between the two copies equals them too, so some adjacent pair is equal; conversely an equal adjacent pair is an equal pair of the input. Merge sort is correct by induction on the merge passes.

shape.note: count depends on the drawn instance; kept so the record says why the diagnostic cannot decide

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(n log n) operations (the depth of any algebraic computation tree that decides element distinctness)
lower_bounds.setting: algebraic computation tree model over the reals: real-valued inputs, arithmetic operations and sign tests at unit cost. Ben-Or's bound is in terms of the number of connected components of the set of yes-inputs; the inputs with pairwise distinct coordinates form n! components (one per ordering).

relationship: Theta(n^2) -> Theta(n log n). Sorting brings equal values together, so n - 1 neighbour comparisons replace n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons. In the algebraic computation tree model on real-valued inputs, Theta(n log n) is optimal (Ben-Or 1983), so sorting-based algorithms are optimal there; the caveats discuss this entry's integer inputs.

sources.title: Lower bounds for algebraic computation trees

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with an independent oracle (len(set(values)) == n, i.e. hashing) on four kinds of inputs (distinct values, distinct values with one planted duplicate, values from [0, n), and distinct values up to 10^18 in magnitude with both signs), n = 0..8, 16, 50, 300 (all pairs up to 300) and 3000, 20000 (sorting). V2 (since 2026-10-07, research/2026-10-07b_count_based_v2.md): on distinct inputs (the all-pairs worst case), the measured quantity is the exact number of COMPARISONS BETWEEN INPUT VALUES (==, <= and the other order operators) made by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented value type (CountingKey in harness.py). All pairs: exactly n(n-1)/2 at n = 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000, 4000 (124750 ... 7998000); alpha = 1.000 against n^2. Sorting: merge-sort comparisons plus the n - 1 neighbour tests, 9710, 21426, 46876, 101729, 219403, 471108, 1006063, 2140632 at n = 1000, 2000, ..., 128000, i.e. n log2 n - c n with c = 0.24 to 0.26; alpha = 1.002 against n log n. The merge part of every count lies within bounds computed from the run lengths alone (sum of min(left, right) <= C <= sum of (left + right - 1)). One seeded instance per n (the sorting count depends on the input order). Tolerance 0.03: exact counts carry no timing noise, so the band only covers lower-order terms (largest |alpha - 1| here 0.002) and stays below half the distance to the nearest rival. Rivals that must NOT fit, all rejected: all pairs against n log n (alpha = 1.757) and n^2 log n (0.936); sorting against n (1.111), n log^2 n (0.912) and n^2 (0.556). So the log factor is resolved for both, which the earlier timing fit could not do (in experiments/2026-10-07_element_distinctness_probe.py the merge-sort timings gave alpha = 1.001 against n log n and 1.125 against n, both inside tolerance 0.25). experiments/2026-10-07b_count_v2_element_distinctness.py reproduces every count above.

caveats: The Omega(n log n) lower bound is a theorem about algebraic computation trees on real-valued inputs; this entry's inputs are integers, and the lower bound does not automatically carry over to models that exploit the representation of integers. On a word RAM, inserting the values into a hash table of size Theta(n) with a function drawn from a universal class (Carter & Wegman 1979) decides distinctness in O(n) expected time: any two distinct keys collide with probability at most 1/(table size), so the expected number of colliding pairs is O(n). That algorithm is randomized and outside the comparison/algebraic model; it is not implemented here (the V1 oracle uses Python's built-in set, whose integer hash is not universal, only as a correctness check). The all-pairs scan is fast when duplicates occur early; its Theta(n^2) is attained exactly on yes-instances.
notes: Element distinctness is a common source of Omega(n log n) lower bounds by reduction (e.g. closest pair: the minimum distance is 0 iff two points coincide; compare pairs/closest-pair-brute-vs-divide-conquer). Its quantum query complexity is a separate topic, not covered by this entry.
